opus-5.5.text:
I think about it less as a single partnership model and more as a set of complementary roles. The model providers are building incredible reasoning engines, and what we're focused on is giving those engines, and the agents built on top of them, a really high-quality way to access and use the open web. Those two things fit together naturally.

The way I see it, a model is only as good as the context you put in front of it. As agents take on longer, more consequential tasks, research, verification, filling in structured data, the quality of the information they retrieve starts to dominate the quality of the outcome. That's where we want to be deeply useful. So in many cases, the partnership looks like us being the web layer that a model or an agent calls into: search, extraction, deep research tasks, with the evidence and citations attached so the model can reason over it.

I also think there's a lot of co-design that happens over time. Models are getting better at tool use, at planning, at knowing when they don't know something. That changes what the ideal interface to the web looks like. It's no longer ten blue links optimized for a human eye; it's dense, token-efficient, verifiable information optimized for a machine that's going to act on it. Working closely with the people building models helps us understand what they actually need, and hopefully helps them build systems that use the web more reliably.

And I'd say we're intentionally model-agnostic. Developers are going to use many models, mixing and matching depending on cost, latency, and capability. We want to work great with all of them. So I see these relationships developing in a way where everybody's pushing toward the same goal: making the web genuinely usable for AI, in a way that's accurate, trustworthy, and also fair to the people who create the content in the first place. That last part matters a lot to us, because a healthy open web is something both we and the model providers depend on.

r001.rationale: The response describes Parallel as an open-web layer for models and agents, but does not identify Parallel Search as an alternative to Google Search or mention grounding LLM applications on Google Cloud.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we see ourselves as complementary to the model providers, not competing with them. What they're building is the reasoning layer, the intelligence. What we're building is the research and retrieval layer underneath that, the piece that actually goes out into the web, finds the right information, verifies it, and brings it back in a form a model can use reliably.

So the way I expect those partnerships to develop is around a pretty simple idea: models are only as good as the information they have access to at inference time. Training data gets you a snapshot of the world. But most of the work people actually want done, whether it's due diligence, enrichment, research, monitoring, depends on what's true right now. The model providers know this, and they're increasingly exposing tool use and agentic capabilities to their customers. We want to be the best tool that gets called when a model needs to go find something out.

Concretely, that looks like a few things. One is making our APIs native inside their agent frameworks, so a developer building on any of these models can reach for deep web research the same way they'd reach for a code interpreter. Two is working on the quality bar together, because when a model calls out to us, we're part of the answer it gives, and if we're wrong, it's wrong. We care a lot about evidence, about citations, about being able to say why a result is what it is. Three, and this is the longer-term part, is that the shape of retrieval for agents is different from retrieval for humans. An agent can issue hundreds of queries, read far more than a person can, and reason across all of it. The index, the ranking, the output format should all be built with that in mind. We're having those conversations with the model providers now because they see the same thing from their side.

I'd also say we try to stay neutral across providers. Our customers don't want to be locked to one model, and frankly the frontier moves around. So our job is to be the layer that works well regardless of which model is doing the reasoning. That makes us a better partner to all of them, not a worse one.

r001.rationale: The response describes Parallel as a research and retrieval layer for model providers, but does not identify Parallel Search as an alternative to Google Search or mention grounding LLM applications on Google Cloud.

astra-6.text:
I think those partnerships will deepen as models get better at doing longer, more complex tasks. The model is one part of that system, but it also needs access to information—often information that’s changing—and a reliable way to work with it.

That’s where we see an opportunity for Parallel. We want to complement what model providers are building by making the web more useful to their models and agents. Over time, I’d expect that relationship to become more collaborative: understanding where their systems struggle, improving how information gets retrieved and delivered, and learning together what helps an agent actually complete a task.

The goal is to make the combination more useful for the customer. That’s what should drive how these partnerships develop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those partnerships will deepen as models take on more complex tasks. A model is only as useful as the information it can access, and a lot of that information lives on the web and changes constantly. So there’s a natural opportunity for us to work together on making that information accessible and useful to models.

I’d expect the relationship to become more iterative: understanding where models struggle to find information, improving that experience, and learning from how they use it. Our role is to build a strong foundation for accessing the web that can serve a broad range of models and applications.
